Five Apple Watch models can measure your blood pressure, alerting you to potential high blood pressure issues. However, they will not provide you with actual blood pressure readings.

Several smart rings and other fitness devices can do this, but they require periodic calibration using a traditional cuff-style blood pressure monitor. The upcoming Signal Ring claims to provide full blood pressure measurements without any calibration, citing a trial involving thousands of people to support this claim...

"Silent Killer"

Both abnormally high blood pressure (hypertension) and low blood pressure (hypotension) can pose significant health risks.

Of the two, high blood pressure is the more dangerous, known as the "silent killer," because it can cause serious and irreversible damage to the arteries, heart, and brain without any obvious symptoms. This condition often goes undetected until it triggers a heart attack or stroke.

Particularly for older adults, regular blood pressure monitoring is a good idea, and home cuff-style blood pressure monitors are also available for self-measurement. However, the ideal scenario is to have fully automatic monitoring through a fitness device you are already wearing.

Apple Watch's Blood Pressure Feature

The launch of watchOS 26 enables five Apple Watch models to measure blood pressure:

  • Apple Watch Series 11
  • Apple Watch Series 10
  • Apple Watch Series 9
  • Apple Watch Ultra 3
  • Apple Watch Ultra 2

However, these devices will not give you any readings, but instead issue an alert when they detect possible signs of high blood pressure. Other devices such as the Oura Ring operate in a similar manner.

Some fitness devices can indeed provide actual blood pressure readings, but they require periodic calibration using readings from a cuff-style blood pressure monitor.

Signal Ring

Startup company Vital Signals claims to have successfully developed a smart ring that can achieve blood pressure measurements as accurate as a traditional upper-arm cuff-style blood pressure monitor without any calibration—this is the Signal Ring.

According to Bloomberg, the company's CEO Tom Moss said he nearly died from undiagnosed high blood pressure, which motivated him to found the company.

The ring will go on presale later today, with shipping in October, priced at US$399, with no subscription required. Real-time blood pressure readings and long-term tracking data will be displayed in the companion app (see image above).

It is worth noting that the Signal Ring has not yet received approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), but clinical trials have shown that it measured accurate blood pressure readings across thousands of participants.

Interestingly, Moss does not intend to sell the ring to everyone—he says these professional features are best suited for older adults and those who have been informed by their doctors of a high blood pressure risk, implying that the Signal Ring may not excel in other areas (such as sleep tracking).
